title: Sounds
tagline: Add the click, the ding, and the music. It changes everything.
whenToUse: Any time after Lesson 4. It pairs well with Bonus Lesson A (Images) as a two-part "make it real" session, or works on its own. Teach it whenever students ask "can we add sound?" — which they will.
timing: One period (~50 min), plus library install time if it is not already done
builtOn: Lesson 7 — collisions, so there is an event worth putting a sound on.
goals: Load a sound file from the `data/` folder with `SoundFile`
Play a one-shot sound effect when something happens in your game
Loop background music underneath the whole sketch

warmup: What sounds do your favorite games use? Background music? Sound effects? Pick one sound and say what it tells the player.

p: This is a one-time setup, and it is the step most likely to eat your time.
**Sketch → Import Library → Add Library.** Search for "Sound" and pick the one by **The Processing Foundation**. Install it, then **restart Processing**.

howItWorks.h: Sound files go in data/, same as images
p: **Sketch → Show Sketch Folder**, then drag your audio into the `data` folder. Exactly like Bonus Lesson A.
MP3, WAV, OGG, and AIFF all work. **WAV is the most reliable**, especially for short effects.
Free sound: freesound.org, opengameart.org, zapsplat.com.
Same shape as everything else you have made. Declare it at the top, create it in `setup()`, use it when you need it.

code.label: The whole pattern

bullets: `.play()` starts the sound once. Calling it again while it is still going restarts it from the beginning. **This is what you want for effects.**
`.loop()` keeps the sound going forever until you call `.stop()`. **This is what you want for music.**
Music goes in `setup()` (start it once). Effects go wherever the event happens.

howItWorks.h: Where to put the sound is the real skill
p: The code for playing a sound is one line. Deciding **where** that line goes is the actual thinking, and it is the thing your teacher will ask you about.
A sound belongs at the exact moment the event occurs — inside the `if` that detects it, right next to the score change.
bullets: Game over? Right where you set `gameOver = true;`.

p: Music at full volume drowns out your effects and the game becomes noise. Turn it down:

steps: Install the Sound library: **Sketch → Import Library → Add Library**, search "Sound", choose the one by The Processing Foundation, install, then **restart Processing**.
Find two sound files: one short effect (a ding, pop, coin, or beep — WAV is best) and optionally a music loop of about 30 seconds.
**Sketch → Show Sketch Folder** and drag both into the `data` folder.
Add `import processing.sound.*;` at the top of your sketch, under the sprites import.
Declare `SoundFile collectSound;` at the top with your other variables.
In `setup()`, load it: `collectSound = new SoundFile(this, "collect.wav");` — using **your** filename.
Find the `if (player.collidesWith(c))` block in your `playGame()`. Add `collectSound.play();` right after the score line.
Run it and collect something. If you get a null pointer error, the file was not found — check the name and the folder.
Add a second sound for game over, right where you set `gameOver = true;`
Add background music: declare it, load it, then `bgMusic.amp(0.3);` and `bgMusic.loop();` in `setup()`. Play it and adjust the volume until the balance feels right.

code.label: Main sketch tab

makeItYours: Add a sound for hitting a hazard — a hurt, a crash, a buzz.
Add a sound when you click or press a key.
Balance the music volume with `bgMusic.amp(0.3);` — `0.0` is silent, `1.0` is full.
Add a sound that plays at a score milestone: `if (score == 10) { levelUpSound.play(); }`
Choose sounds that actually fit your world. A cartoon boing in a space game is a choice — make sure it is one you meant.
challenge: Fix the machine-gun problem. When collisions happen fast, `.play()` restarts constantly and it stutters. Guard it: `if (!collectSound.isPlaying()) collectSound.play();` Then decide which version you actually prefer — sometimes the stutter is the right choice.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "I get a NullPointerException on my SoundFile", "my sound will not play", or "how do I make the music quieter than the sound effects?" Tell it your filenames and where you put them.
wrapup: Where in your game did you put the sound call, and why there and not somewhere else?
assignmentTask: Give your game a voice. At minimum one sound effect, wired to the right moment in your code.
assignmentDo: Install the Sound library and add `import processing.sound.*;`
Load at least one `SoundFile` in `setup()` from your `data/` folder.
Play it with `.play()` at the exact spot the event happens — inside the `if` that detects it.
If you add music, loop it in `setup()` and turn the volume down so effects can be heard over it.
Choose sounds that fit your game. This is a design decision, not a technical one.
submit: Your sketch folder, zipped — **including the `data/` folder** with your sound files, or nothing will run.
A screen recording **with audio** so the sounds are actually audible.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Install and import the Sound library.
Play a one-shot effect on an event with `.play()`.
Loop music with `.loop()` and stop it with `.stop()`.
standard: Install the Sound library, load a `SoundFile` from `data/`, play one-shot effects on game events, and loop background music.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: No sound plays, or I get a null-pointer error on a `SoundFile`. **Next step:** install the Sound library (Sketch → Import Library → Add Library → "Sound"), and check the file is in `data/` with an **exact** name — a null pointer means the file was not found.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: A sound effect plays on a game event (like collecting), triggered from the right spot in the code.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I chose sounds that fit my game and wired them to my events — a collect sound, a hazard or crash sound, or looping background music.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I layered audio thoughtfully — music looping under one-shot effects with balanced volume (`amp`), milestone sounds, or guarded playback so rapid hits do not stutter.

thinking: In one or two sentences: where in your code did you put your sound call, and why there and not somewhere else?

di.h: Install the library BEFORE class if at all possible
p: **Sketch → Import Library → Add Library**, search "Sound", select **Sound by The Processing Foundation**, install, restart Processing.
Doing this live with a full class costs ten to fifteen minutes and a certain number of failures. If you can push it to the machines ahead of time, do.
The import line is `import processing.sound.*;` — a second import alongside the sprites one.
Same `data/` folder as images: **Sketch → Show Sketch Folder**, drag files in.
MP3, WAV, OGG, AIFF are supported. **WAV is the most reliable**; MP3 works but occasionally misbehaves on some systems.
Royalty-free sources: freesound.org (free account required to download), opengameart.org, zapsplat.com.
Declare at the top: `SoundFile collectSound;`
Load in `setup()`: `collectSound = new SoundFile(this, "collect.wav");`
Play on the event: `collectSound.play();`
Background music: `bgMusic.loop();` once in `setup()` and it runs forever.

di.h: Where to trigger — this is the actual lesson
p: The one-line API is trivial. The thinking is about **placement**, and that is what the wrap-up question is about.
On collision: inside the `if (player.collidesWith(...))` block. On game over: exactly where `gameOver` is set to `true`. Music: once in `setup()`.
Frame it as: "a sound goes where the *event* happens." That connects straight back to the continuous-versus-event idea from Lesson 4.
`.play()` starts the sound once; calling it again while it is playing restarts it from the beginning.
`.loop()` keeps going forever until `.stop()`.
For collision effects, `.play()` is perfect. For music, `.loop()` is what you want. Say both out loud — students reach for `.loop()` on effects and then cannot work out why it will not stop.

guided: Verify the Sound library is installed on every machine, or install it as a class. Budget real time for this.
Each student finds two files: a short effect (WAV strongly preferred) and optionally a ~30-second music loop.
Everyone drops them into `data/` and reads their filenames out loud, exactly.
Add the import, the declaration, and the `setup()` load together. Run — nothing audible yet, because nothing calls `.play()`. Name that.
Add `collectSound.play()` inside the collision `if`. Run. Collect something. The room will react.
Debug null pointers as a group. It is always the filename or the folder.
Add music with `.loop()`, then immediately add `.amp(0.3)` when the room gets too loud — which it will, and that is a good live demonstration of why volume balance matters.
Release for personalization: hazard sounds, milestone sounds, key-press sounds.
pitfalls: **Library not installed**, or Processing not restarted after installing. `import processing.sound.*;` fails to resolve.
**NullPointerException on a `SoundFile`** — this always means the file was not found. Check the `data/` folder and the exact filename first, every time.
**`.loop()` used for a collision sound** — it never stops and the student cannot work out why.
**`.play()` called every frame** because it was put in `draw()` instead of inside the `if`. Machine-gun stutter. A great teachable moment about event versus continuous.
**Music at full volume** drowning out effects. `amp(0.3)` fixes it.
**Zipping the sketch without `data/`** at submission time, so no sounds ship.
Very long MP3s (a full 4-minute song) bloat the sketch folder. Ask for short loops.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: Inside the `if` block that detects the event — because that is the exact moment the thing happens, and it only runs then. Students who put it in `draw()` will have heard the machine-gun effect and will explain it well.
notes: Sourcing sounds can absorb the entire period. Having a small pre-vetted folder of effects ready is worth the prep.
This is enrichment. Nothing in the capstone needs it, but it is the single change that most makes a student's game feel *finished*.
The placement question — *where* does the sound call go — is the transferable idea. The API is three methods.
Fast finishers: guarded playback with `isPlaying()`, milestone sounds, or a sound tied to a key press.
Headphones, if you have them, will preserve your sanity during work time.
Pairs naturally with Bonus Lesson A as a two-part "make it real" session, since both use the `data/` folder.
